hero.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI courtroom rules requiring lawyers to verify citations amid rampant misuse
hero.body:
Starting June 15, Florida attorneys and people representing themselves in court must certify that any citations they submit are accurate and actually exist. The Florida Supreme Court recently established these new rules to combat what legal professionals describe as a serious and growing problem: artificial intelligence generating false legal citations and fabricated evidence in courtrooms. Violations could result in sanctions ranging from public reprimand to fines and suspension from practice.

Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has worked to address AI misuse in his courtroom after witnessing the problem firsthand. He expressed concern that the situation will worsen before it improves, though he believes the Florida Supreme Court's action will help the state. Criminal defense attorney Paul Figueroa in Tampa, who recently began using AI to enhance his practice, emphasized that the technology is unreliable. He explained that AI can generate quotes appearing directly relevant to a case that actually do not appear in the cited cases. When asked if the new rules are sufficient, Figueroa said they go far enough for current circumstances.

One notable case involved a Polk County attorney representing the school district in litigation over school bus cameras. A judge discovered the attorney had included fabricated facts and cited cases that do not exist in a motion to dismiss. The attorney apologized and acknowledged using ChatGPT as a research and drafting tool, admitting there was no valid reason for failing to verify the information before filing. The school district stated it takes accuracy and legal integrity seriously and is reviewing whether to continue using this attorney for future work.

The problems with AI-generated false evidence have become widespread enough to demand the court's action. Earlier this year, a St. Petersburg woman created a fake photo using AI, claiming a man had robbed and assaulted her, though she later confessed to police that she fabricated the allegation. Judge Matthewman warned both lawyers and self-represented litigants to carefully verify everything they file with the court. He cautioned that failing to do so could result in serious consequences.

cards.headline: Florida Voters to Decide Property Tax Cut as Legislature Sends Homestead Exemption to November Ballot
cards.body:
Florida residents will have the opportunity to vote in November on a constitutional amendment that would significantly expand homestead property tax exemptions. The proposal has advanced through both chambers of the state legislature with substantial support, though local government officials have raised concerns about the financial consequences. The Senate approved the measure 30-9, following a House vote of 75-26. The amendment is a priority initiative for Governor Ron DeSantis.

The constitutional amendment would increase homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 if voters approve it by the required 60% margin. The measure would apply to homeowners who own primary residences in Florida by the end of this year. Future increases would be indexed to the Consumer Price Index. However, school property taxes would remain exempt from these higher limits and would continue to be subject only to the current $25,000 exemption threshold. This distinction means that while homeowners would see relief on county and municipal taxes, their school tax obligations would not increase at the same rate.

County and city officials have warned that the amendment could create significant budget challenges for local governments, though the exact financial impact is still being calculated. The uncertainty about potential revenue losses has left questions about where budget cuts might occur if voters approve the measure. Some local leaders have suggested that reduced funding could affect municipal services. A similar proposal to expand homestead exemptions failed when presented to voters in 2018, making this the latest attempt to provide tax relief to Florida homeowners. The tradeoff between providing tax relief and maintaining funding for local services remains a central point of debate surrounding the amendment.

The measure represents an ongoing effort to reduce property tax burdens on Florida residents who own their primary homes. As the legislature has moved the amendment forward, it has secured backing from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers, indicating broader support for some form of property tax relief. However, the path forward depends on whether Florida voters believe the benefits of expanded homestead exemptions outweigh concerns about reduced local government revenue. When the constitutional amendment appears on the November ballot, voters will make the final determination about whether to implement these significant changes to Florida's property tax system.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island faces critical erosion threatening to split island at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean potentially breaking through at Peck Lake and splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development is already at risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. According to the report, sites at risk include the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field acknowledged the approach is temporary, saying "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over. We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." He said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment annually.

cards.headline: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings Suspends Campaign for Governor After Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
cards.teaser: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings is ending his gubernatorial campaign after receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis this week, announcing he will focus on treatment and serving the remaining six months of his term.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

Jerry Demings is suspending his campaign for Governor after receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis on Monday. He informed his children of his decision to quit the campaign on Thursday. Demings said he plans to complete his remaining six months as Orange County Mayor, stating he intends to "run through the finish line" in that role. "In order for me to receive the treatment that I need, I am going to have to come off the campaign trail," Demings said. "I have to let something go. I can't continue to do my job as Mayor, take care of my family and run for Governor. So, I made a difficult decision."

Demings expressed optimism about his prognosis while highlighting the prevalence of prostate cancer among men. He noted that 1 in 6 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer, with the rate climbing to 1 in 4 for African American men. The suspension removes one candidate from Florida's gubernatorial race as the state approaches the election cycle.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split barrier island at Peck Lake, state report warns
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report documents severe erosion along nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island, threatening infrastructure, ecosystems, and historical sites. The 11.5-mile shoreline has deteriorated to a critical point where ocean water could potentially break through at Peck Lake and split the barrier island in half. This threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development already faces risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach would convert the thin strip of land into an open inlet. A similar breach occurred in the early 1960s during a storm before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers restored the area by adding sand.

According to Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society, another breach would damage fragile ecosystems that depend on a precise balance between fresh and saltwater environments. He warned that increasing storm surge frequency could create additional breaks in coastal protection. The consequences would extend far beyond the immediate shoreline. The report identifies multiple sites at risk, including the Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site estimated to be 3,000 to 4,000 years old that has already lost half its structure to erosion. Conservation lands like Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park also face danger. Perry noted that more than 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A second state assessment warns that erosion threatens mangrove swamps that provide critical habitat and coastal protection, while rising water levels could displace entire species populations on the island.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field acknowledged the seriousness of the situation while describing the town's ongoing response. The community continues fighting erosion through regular maintenance projects. In April 2025, Jupiter Island completed a major beach renourishment effort that deposited sand equivalent to filling nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field stressed that oceanfront homes currently face no immediate danger only because of this continuous work. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. "We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it."

The town invests approximately 3 million dollars annually in beach renourishment from local taxpayer funds. However, this funding stream remains uncertain. If the island were to breach, repairs would likely require substantial state and federal investment. Field cautioned that "if funding ever goes away for beach renourishment in Florida, the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with." The recent state assessment may help Jupiter Island compete more effectively for state and federal funding to address erosion and protect its communities and natural resources.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie resident's home security camera captures burglary in progress, suspect arrested
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A man was arrested Thursday afternoon after a Port St. Lucie resident's home security camera caught him burglarizing an apartment in real time. Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following the incident at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail.

The incident began around 3:38 p.m. when the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. Checking his live camera feed, he spotted a masked man inside his apartment and activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly before returning to tamper with the camera. Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. When Port St. Lucie Police arrived, they found clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary. Thibodeau was transported to the St. Lucie County jail.

hero.headline: Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties enforce fertilizer ban starting Monday
hero.body:
Beginning Monday, June 30, residents across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop applying fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen to their lawns and landscaping. The seasonal restriction takes effect as the rainy season begins and will remain in place through the end of summer. The ban aims to curb nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways, where excess nutrients trigger harmful algae blooms in areas like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Environmental Resources staff in St. Lucie County explain the reasoning behind the restriction. According to Jordan Skaggs with the county's Environmental Resources division, these algae blooms pose multiple threats to the aquatic ecosystem. The dense growth can block sunlight from reaching underwater vegetation that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. Beyond ecological concerns, harmful algae blooms become particularly dangerous at high concentrations, as they can produce toxins harmful to human health, animal populations, and the overall health of waterways and surrounding ecosystems.

Rather than leaving lawns and gardens without nutrient support during the ban period, University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences offers a practical alternative. Grantly Ricketts, director of the St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective way to add nutrients to landscaping without violating fertilizer restrictions. Composting requires minimal equipment and can work in residential settings using something as simple as a small trash can, making it accessible to most homeowners. This method allows residents to recycle organic materials while still maintaining healthy gardens and landscaping throughout the restricted months.

The fertilizer ban applies broadly across all three counties, affecting every residential property with a lawn or landscaping. Local officials emphasize that composting provides both an environmentally responsible solution and a practical way to care for yards during the rainy season. By switching to composting methods now, residents can help reduce the nutrient pollution flowing into waterways while maintaining their landscapes naturally.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax ballot measure ahead of November vote
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass, the same threshold that defeated a similar proposal in 2018. How much money cities and counties would lose under the plan remains under calculation, and it is unknown where budget cuts would fall if the measure passes.

Brian Edington supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. He is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood's trash services as an example, saying twice-weekly pickup is unnecessary when once weekly would be adequate. Rosabella Olivares, a West Palm Beach shopper, expressed concern about reduced funding, saying everything is expensive now. While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed more skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach renters and predicted landlords would raise rent instead.

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks for 250th anniversary due to drought
cards.teaser: State leaders are watching drought conditions closely as they weigh whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence, with the entire state at least abnormally dry.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders weigh whether to ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing a range of moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban in May, stating that if drought conditions persist through the Fourth of July, a ban is possible. Simpson warned that hundreds of thousands of people doing fireworks could put the entire state on fire all at one time. He acknowledged the significance of this year's holiday but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity ahead of the holiday. Murphy said the store monitors drought conditions carefully and keeps a close eye on the drought index to ensure the ground is saturated enough, though he noted plenty of rain is in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed as demand outpaces funding
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month, but has only about $2 million in combined grant funding available.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program, which has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding, is overwhelmed by demand for help. Applications open at the beginning of each month and fill quickly, with the program typically receiving about 600 applications within the first couple of hours. Currently, about 800 applications are in the queue for rental assistance. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Program director Dr. James Green said there are nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month based on combined data with 211. He urged anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

The surge in applications stems partly from rising costs of living including housing, gas, and food. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, switched careers from a 12-year career as an educator to real estate in hopes of earning more income to afford rent. She said she worries about paying rent almost every day because all bills are rising except paychecks. Green said preventing homelessness depends on everyone and called on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart, claims live worms found in SpaghettiOs caused parasitic infection
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard says she and her daughter developed parasitic infections after buying SpaghettiOs at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee in June 2024.
cards.body:
A woman from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after claiming she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs. Mary Hubbard alleges that she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications following the incident. She purchased the SpaghettiOs in June 2024 from the Walmart Supercenter store located on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee, according to the complaint.

Hubbard's attorneys said she discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. The complaint states that Hubbard documented the contamination in multiple videos, which clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product. The lawsuit alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product and seeks $50,000 in damages. Campbell said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban, warn of economic impact to conservation businesses
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast within 200 miles is drawing criticism from the state's shark diving industry, including operators who say it could devastate tourism businesses.
cards.body:
A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry. The measure, H.R. 3831, also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible encounters with sharks, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has yet asked them to present data or explain their practices.

Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, arguing this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties face millions in losses under property tax proposal
cards.teaser: A Florida Association of Counties study estimates Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29 if voters approve a referendum to raise homestead exemptions.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential losses for Treasure Coast counties. Martin County faces $50 million in losses in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County estimates losses of $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if there is a cut in property taxes, there will be real shortfalls and some revenue will have to be made up somewhere. Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possibilities, though officials do not yet know if it will be an increase in sales tax or user fees for other services.

The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal is more of a break for struggling families in a $300,000 home working several jobs to make ends meet. In Palm Beach County, it is estimated that over half of the properties have the homestead exemption, higher than the state average of 47 percent.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach to make way for mixed-use development
cards.teaser: Crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
This week, crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall to make way for a revitalization project. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager on the redevelopment, said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's and soon the former Sears location. Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she is happy about the change because the mall has degraded over time. Mark Manera, who has been visiting the mall for years, described it as a graveyard that experienced a steady decline year after year and said change is needed.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described the project as a city within a city that will replace the dead mall that has been getting cobwebs for the last 12 years. Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027. The team is still working on permitting for the rest of the project.

The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development is already at risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. According to the report, sites at risk include the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field acknowledged the approach is temporary, saying "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over. We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." He said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment annually.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over contaminated SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections after finding live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.
cards.body:
A woman from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in their SpaghettiOs. Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications following the incident. She purchased the SpaghettiOs in June 2024 at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the lawsuit, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food and documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the product.

The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Stuart representative supports property tax cut despite county revenue losses
cards.teaser: State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said he is happy voters will decide on a proposal to raise homestead exemptions, which would benefit struggling families in $300,000 homes.
cards.body:
State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the property tax proposal is more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet. Overdorf said he is happy that there is a proposal out to the voters and they can make a decision with it. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 if approved by voters in November. The savings for homeowners can vary from the hundreds to the thousands, depending on the county and city and the assessed value of a home.

Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. According to a study from the Florida Association of Counties, the referendum could cost Palm Beach County $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29. Martin County would lose an estimated $50 million and $93 million in those same periods, while St. Lucie County could see losses of $80 million and $140 million. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said local officials may need to find new revenue sources or make budget cuts to offset potential shortfalls. In Palm Beach County, it is estimated that over half of the properties have the homestead exemption, higher than the state average of 47%.

cards.headline: Florida may ban Fourth of July fireworks due to severe drought
cards.teaser: Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned that if drought conditions persist, the state could ban fireworks for the 250th anniversary of American independence.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look significantly different this year as state leaders weigh whether to ban fireworks due to severe drought conditions. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was implemented. The entire state is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of a ban in May, noting that if drought conditions persist through the Fourth of July, a ban could occur. Simpson cautioned that potentially hundreds of thousands of people setting off fireworks could put the entire state on fire. He acknowledged the significance of the 250th anniversary of American independence but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, customer activity has already increased ahead of the holiday. Store manager Bill Murphy said the business monitors the drought index closely to ensure adequate ground saturation but remains cautiously optimistic, citing rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

hero.headline: West Palm Beach residents divided on property tax referendum ahead of November vote
hero.teaser: Florida voters will decide in November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents.
hero.body:
Florida voters will decide in November whether to increase the homestead exemption, a proposal that would reduce property taxes for homeowners. The referendum requires 60% voter approval to pass. This marks the second time such a measure has appeared on the ballot, as a similar homestead exemption proposal failed to gain sufficient support in 2018. Officials are still calculating how much funding cities and counties would lose under this plan, and the specific areas that might face budget cuts remain unclear.

Support for the measure among homeowners centers on reducing their tax burden. Brian Edington backs the proposal because he believes it primarily benefits Floridians who live in the state permanently rather than part-time residents. Edington said he is comfortable with local governments spending less money and offered his own neighborhood as an example of where reductions could occur. He noted that his area receives trash pickup twice weekly but could function adequately with weekly service instead. Another resident suggested that property taxes should be more directly tied to the services people actually use, arguing that those with children in school should pay more while those without school-age children could pay less.

Not all homeowners embrace the measure without reservations. A resident identified as Stan expressed concern that funding should not be eliminated entirely, particularly for infrastructure. He indicated willingness to support a reduction that would help residents while maintaining necessary services. Rosabella Olivares raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced government funding, pointing out that costs for providing services are currently high and that less money would complicate municipal operations.

Renters voiced particular skepticism about the proposal's benefits. A renter along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach expressed doubt that savings would extend to the rental community. This resident predicted that landlords would raise rents in response to their own reduced property tax bills, meaning renters would not experience any financial relief from the measure. The division between homeowners and renters reflects broader concerns about who ultimately benefits from the tax reduction and how it might affect the broader community's ability to fund essential services and infrastructure.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $32 million loss under property tax referendum
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29 if voters approve a property tax reform referendum that raises the homestead exemption, according to a Florida Association of Counties study.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties offered estimates of potential losses for area counties. Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Martin County faces $50 million in losses in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29.

The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. The savings for homeowners can vary from the hundreds to the thousands, depending on the county and city and the assessed value of a home. Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal offers "a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet."

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell addresses $280 million property tax impact
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said officials are working to determine the impact of property tax reform that could cost the county $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29.
cards.body: Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said county officials are working with the Office of Management and Budget to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. According to a recent study from the Florida Association of Counties, Palm Beach County could lose $280 million in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29 if the referendum passes. Powell acknowledged that property tax cuts would create real shortfalls and challenges, requiring officials to find new revenue sources elsewhere. Like all local officials, Powell is restricted by state law from speaking against or endorsing the referendum, but he can provide educational information about it. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. In Palm Beach County, over half of properties have the homestead exemption, which is higher than the state average of 47%. Voters will decide on the referendum in November.

cards.headline: Stuart lawmaker supports homestead exemption increase on November ballot
cards.teaser: State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said he is happy voters will decide on a property tax proposal that he says provides a break for struggling families in $300,000 homes working several jobs to make ends meet.
cards.body:
State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the referendum to raise the homestead exemption is more of a break for the struggling family that is in a $300,000 home and working several jobs to make sure ends meet. He said he is happy that there is a proposal out to the voters and they can make a decision with it.

The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Voters will decide the measure in November. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential revenue losses, including $280 million in Palm Beach County in 2027-28 and $523 million in 2028-29. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said local officials are working with the Office of Management and Budget to determine the impact. He noted that if property taxes are cut, there will be real shortfalls and challenges, and revenue will have to be made up somewhere, potentially through increased sales tax or user fees for services.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach for mixed-use redevelopment
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center.
cards.body:
Crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said the first phase involves taking down Macy's and the former Sears location. Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she was happy about the teardown because the mall had degraded over time. Mark Manera, a longtime visitor to the mall, described it as looking like "the death of a beautiful building" and compared it to a graveyard, noting a steady decline year after year.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center featuring around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. "They're not going to see a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs," Scarfone said, calling it "a city within a city." Manera said the change was needed and expressed hope that it would bring new life, jobs and opportunities. Scarfone said he hopes to complete the first phase by 2027, though the team is still working on permitting for the rest of the project.

cards.headline: Vero Beach resident calls Indian River Mall a graveyard before demolition
cards.teaser: Mark Manera from Vero Beach said the Indian River Mall was more like a graveyard with a steady decline year after year as he watched crews begin tearing down the shopping center.
cards.body:
Crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager for the redevelopment, said the first phase involves taking down the Macy's and soon the former Sears location.

Neighbors watching the demolition shared mixed perspectives on the changes. Mark Manera from Vero Beach, who has visited the mall for years, described it as "a graveyard" and noted "a steady decline year after year after year." He said change is needed and that if redevelopment brings "new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful." Mary Alice Stopyra, another neighbor at the demolition site, said she is "really happy they're tearing this down" because "it's just degraded over time." Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. "They're not going to see a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs," Scarfone said. He hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, while the team continues working on permitting for the remaining project phases.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County property tax losses could reach $140 million by 2028
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29 if voters approve a property tax reform referendum in November, according to a Florida Association of Counties study.
cards.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of a property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to a recent study from the Florida Association of Counties, St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29 if voters approve the measure in November. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said local officials are restricted by the state from speaking out against or endorsing the referendum but can offer educational information about it.

If the referendum passes, local governments may face significant revenue shortfalls that could require new revenue sources or budget cuts. "We don't know if it will be an increase in sales tax, we don't know if it will be an increase in user fees for other services," Powell said. The savings for homeowners can vary from the hundreds to the thousands, depending on the county, city and the assessed value of a home. Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice Musical Runs Through Saturday at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
hero.teaser: The Broadway hit musical based on Tim Burton's 1988 film plays through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, with tickets starting at $34.50.
hero.body:
Beetlejuice the musical is now playing at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon beloved from Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. He gets to break the fourth wall a lot and communicate directly to the audience. Very early in the run, he experienced an unexpected moment when a wig change went wrong. He was wearing two wigs and the second wig came off with the first wig, so he was bald for an entire scene.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50, and the safest and most secure way to get them is to buy directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Over 100 Paddlers to Cross 80 Miles of Ocean for Cystic Fibrosis, Arriving at Lake Worth Beach June 13
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the Atlantic Ocean this June to raise funds for families living with cystic fibrosis during the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Event founder Travis Suit said participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The crossing benefits the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit established in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. The four-day event begins June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove, followed by a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner on Thursday. Friday features a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony honoring cystic fibrosis warriors, with safety checks before the midnight launch.

All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours, and GPS trackers provided by the event must remain active throughout the crossing. Mandatory safety meetings will be held. Individual paddlers must raise at least $2,000, while crew and virtual participants have a $500 minimum, with final contributions due by July 31. Suit created the event after learning about the respiratory benefits of ocean salt air. The foundation now provides direct support to cystic fibrosis patients and families, connecting them with resources and community. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong celebration welcoming the arriving paddlers.

hero.headline: Florida Voters to Decide Property Tax Cut as Legislature Sends Homestead Exemption to November Ballot
hero.body:
Florida residents will have the opportunity to vote in November on a constitutional amendment that would significantly expand homestead property tax exemptions. The proposal has advanced through both chambers of the state legislature with substantial support, though local government officials have raised concerns about the financial consequences. The Senate approved the measure 30-9, following a House vote of 75-26. The amendment is a priority initiative for Governor Ron DeSantis.

The constitutional amendment would increase homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 if voters approve it by the required 60% margin. The measure would apply to homeowners who own primary residences in Florida by the end of this year. Future increases would be indexed to the Consumer Price Index. However, school property taxes would remain exempt from these higher limits and would continue to be subject only to the current $25,000 exemption threshold. This distinction means that while homeowners would see relief on county and municipal taxes, their school tax obligations would not increase at the same rate.

County and city officials have warned that the amendment could create significant budget challenges for local governments, though the exact financial impact is still being calculated. The uncertainty about potential revenue losses has left questions about where budget cuts might occur if voters approve the measure. Some local leaders have suggested that reduced funding could affect municipal services. A similar proposal to expand homestead exemptions failed when presented to voters in 2018, making this the latest attempt to provide tax relief to Florida homeowners. The tradeoff between providing tax relief and maintaining funding for local services remains a central point of debate surrounding the amendment.

The measure represents an ongoing effort to reduce property tax burdens on Florida residents who own their primary homes. As the legislature has moved the amendment forward, it has secured backing from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers, indicating broader support for some form of property tax relief. However, the path forward depends on whether Florida voters believe the benefits of expanded homestead exemptions outweigh concerns about reduced local government revenue. When the constitutional amendment appears on the November ballot, voters will make the final determination about whether to implement these significant changes to Florida's property tax system.

cards.headline: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings Suspends Campaign for Governor After Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
cards.teaser: Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings is ending his gubernatorial campaign after receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis this week, announcing he will focus on treatment and serving the remaining six months of his term.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

Jerry Demings is suspending his campaign for Governor after receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis on Monday. He informed his children of his decision to quit the campaign on Thursday. Demings said he plans to complete his remaining six months as Orange County Mayor, stating he intends to "run through the finish line" in that role. "In order for me to receive the treatment that I need, I am going to have to come off the campaign trail," Demings said. "I have to let something go. I can't continue to do my job as Mayor, take care of my family and run for Governor. So, I made a difficult decision."

Demings expressed optimism about his prognosis while highlighting the prevalence of prostate cancer among men. He noted that 1 in 6 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer, with the rate climbing to 1 in 4 for African American men. The suspension removes one candidate from Florida's gubernatorial race as the state approaches the election cycle.

cards.headline: President Trump Nominates Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez as U.S. Ambassador to Brazil
cards.teaser: House Speaker Daniel Perez, who spent two years leading the Florida House and publicly battling Governor DeSantis, may soon head to South America after receiving a presidential nomination.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump has nominated Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez as U.S. Ambassador to Brazil, the largest country in South America and one of the United States' most significant trade and diplomatic partners in the region. The nomination was part of a broader batch of appointments Trump sent to the Senate, which also included four other Florida nominees for ambassador and federal law enforcement posts.

Perez spent the past two years leading the Florida House, publicly battling DeSantis while moving the Legislature toward a more coequal footing. The nomination comes just under nine months after the White House urged Perez to run for Florida Attorney General, an undertaking he declined to pursue that would have put him on a collision course with DeSantis appointee James Uthmeier.

cards.headline: Florida Shark Diving Operators Fight Federal Feeding Ban as Bill Clears House
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding in waters off Florida has drawn opposition from dive operators who say it unfairly targets conservation-focused businesses while leaving fishing practices untouched.
cards.body:
A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry, with operators warning it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses while doing little to curb safety risks. The measure, H.R. 3831, also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House. It would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. A coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, which often includes veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible encounters with sharks, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said the industry is requesting the chance to speak and share the science and the facts, noting that no one from Congress has yet asked operators to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, arguing this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food.

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent. However, Florida operators and some researchers say the Hawaii experience tells a different story. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch.

cards.headline: Florida State University Graduates First Leon County Veterans from Entrepreneurship Certificate Program
cards.teaser: Fourteen veterans completed a six-week business training program at FSU's Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship, joining a statewide network of more than 2,700 Florida business owners.
cards.body:
Florida State University's Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship graduated the first Leon County cohort of its Veteran Entrepreneurship Certificate Program this week through a partnership with Veterans Florida. Fourteen veterans completed the six-week Facilitated Business Modeling Program, which focuses on customer discovery, market validation and entrepreneurial decision-making. Participants included both aspiring entrepreneurs with early-stage concepts and business owners looking to refine and grow existing operations.

Eric Liguori, associate dean for Research and External Relations at the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship, led the program and noted that veterans bring resilience, leadership and adaptability to entrepreneurship. The program combined workshops, mentoring and applied exercises designed to help participants evaluate opportunities and strengthen business concepts. Veterans also connected with local entrepreneurial resources and learned from FSU faculty members including Susana Santos, Bill Lickson, Juliana Binhote, Doug Tatum and Melissa Robert. Graduates received certificates of completion and are now eligible to join the Jim Moran Institute for Global Entrepreneurship's statewide alumni network of more than 2,700 Florida business owners. Dean Susan Fiorito said the partnership with Veterans Florida reflects community-centered impact and supports veterans and military-connected families pursuing entrepreneurial opportunities.

cards.headline: Republican Byron Donalds Raises $81.1 Million for Florida Governor Campaign
cards.teaser: U.S. Representative Byron Donalds has raised approximately $81.1 million for his run for Governor of Florida, according to campaign finance reports.
cards.body:
Republican Byron Donalds has raised approximately $81.1 million for his gubernatorial campaign, according to campaign finance data. Of that total, $13.8 million came in April and May alone. The Naples Congressman's official campaign account has raised $9.2 million through May, with more than $2.13 million of that arriving after the first quarter. The account has received donations from over 8,812 people. His Friends of Byron Donalds political committee has reported over $71.8 million in total contributions, with $11.7 million raised in the last two months.

Donalds has consistently outraised other GOP candidates in the gubernatorial race, bolstered by early support from President Donald Trump. The $81.1 million figure represents combined fundraising from both his official campaign account, which operates under stricter contribution limits, and his political committee. The substantial war chest demonstrates the resources being mobilized in Florida's race for Governor.

cards.headline: Gatorland Opens New Craft Beer Bar with Exclusive Brew from Winter Garden's Crooked Can Brewery
cards.teaser: The Orlando theme park opened the Guzzlin' Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend, featuring an exclusive lager that can only be found at the park.
cards.body:
To celebrate the start of summer, Gatorland opened the Guzzlin' Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend, an outdoor, shaded bar featuring an exclusive craft beer made by Winter Garden's Crooked Can Brewery. The Grinnin' Gator lager can only be found at the park and represents a partnership between Florida's attractions and local breweries. The beverage barn serves the Grinnin' Gator on tap along with five other pours, including offerings from Orlando's Ivanhoe Park and Orange Blossom breweries. Additional drinks are available in cans.

Tim Acheson, Gatorland's Director of Food and Beverage, approached his friend at Crooked Can Brewery to develop the specialty beer. Crooked Can settled on a Pale German lager with hints of citrus. Alan Delahunt, Managing Partner at Crooked Can Brewing Company, said they wanted to provide "a beer that was kind of a beer for everybody, which is why we landed on that pale lager." The space, located near the Legends of the Swamp show, is meant to give guests a place to relax in the heat. For Crooked Can, working with Gatorland follows specialty brews for the Orlando Magic, Disney World's Epcot festivals, and Universal Orlando Resort. The Grinnin' Gator is served in a plastic cup, but Gatorland will sell six-packs in the gift shop for guests to take home with decorative cans.

hero.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split barrier island at Peck Lake, state report warns
hero.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report documents severe erosion along nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island, threatening infrastructure, ecosystems, and historical sites. The 11.5-mile shoreline has deteriorated to a critical point where ocean water could potentially break through at Peck Lake and split the barrier island in half. This threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development already faces risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach would convert the thin strip of land into an open inlet. A similar breach occurred in the early 1960s during a storm before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers restored the area by adding sand.

According to Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society, another breach would damage fragile ecosystems that depend on a precise balance between fresh and saltwater environments. He warned that increasing storm surge frequency could create additional breaks in coastal protection. The consequences would extend far beyond the immediate shoreline. The report identifies multiple sites at risk, including the Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site estimated to be 3,000 to 4,000 years old that has already lost half its structure to erosion. Conservation lands like Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park also face danger. Perry noted that more than 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A second state assessment warns that erosion threatens mangrove swamps that provide critical habitat and coastal protection, while rising water levels could displace entire species populations on the island.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field acknowledged the seriousness of the situation while describing the town's ongoing response. The community continues fighting erosion through regular maintenance projects. In April 2025, Jupiter Island completed a major beach renourishment effort that deposited sand equivalent to filling nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field stressed that oceanfront homes currently face no immediate danger only because of this continuous work. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. "We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it."

The town invests approximately 3 million dollars annually in beach renourishment from local taxpayer funds. However, this funding stream remains uncertain. If the island were to breach, repairs would likely require substantial state and federal investment. Field cautioned that "if funding ever goes away for beach renourishment in Florida, the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly, and not in a way that anybody's particularly happy with." The recent state assessment may help Jupiter Island compete more effectively for state and federal funding to address erosion and protect its communities and natural resources.

cards.headline: Summer fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: Residents cannot use fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns or landscaping from June 1 through September 30. The ban aims to reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season that can cause algae blooms.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have implemented a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen from June 1 through September 30. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban is designed to reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms that disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

According to Skaggs, algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on. At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an alternative during the ban period. Ricketts said composting can work like a small trash can and is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to landscaping and gardens.

cards.headline: Martin County revamps emergency dispatch center
cards.teaser: Martin County has upgraded its emergency dispatch center.
cards.body: Martin County has completed a revamp of its emergency dispatch center. The improvements were made to the county's 911 operations facility.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguishes nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue responded to a large brush fire in Indiantown that burned nearly 40 acres.
cards.body: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a brush fire in Indiantown that covered nearly 40 acres. The fire was brought under control by county firefighters.

cards.teaser: A brief law enforcement pursuit slowed northbound traffic on Interstate 95 near Hobe Sound.

cards.teaser: Stuart Bell, a finalist for University of Florida president, spoke about diversity, equity and inclusion issues at a public forum.
cards.body: Stuart Bell, one of the finalists for University of Florida president, addressed concerns about diversity, equity and inclusion during a public forum. Bell fielded questions from attendees about his approach to DEI policies at the university.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties
hero.teaser: Starting June 1, residents cannot use fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns or landscaping through the rainy season.
hero.body:
Starting June 1 and continuing through September 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will be restricted from using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The seasonal prohibition targets the months when rainfall is heaviest in the region, aiming to prevent nutrient-laden runoff from entering local waterways during the rainy season.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban exists to combat a significant environmental problem. When fertilizers wash into rivers and lagoons during heavy rains, they can trigger algae blooms that damage aquatic ecosystems. The Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River are particularly vulnerable to these blooms, which can disrupt the delicate balance of these waterways and harm the species that depend on them.

The consequences of harmful algae blooms extend beyond environmental damage. Skaggs explained that these blooms can shade out plants that fish and wildlife rely on for survival. In some cases, when algae blooms reach high concentrations, they produce toxins that pose serious threats. These toxins can endanger human health, harm wildlife populations, and degrade the overall health of the ecosystem.

For residents looking to maintain their gardens and landscaping during the ban period, Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective alternative. Ricketts noted that composting can be as simple as using a small container and represents one of the easiest and most practical methods available to add necessary nutrients to landscaping without relying on commercial fertilizers. By turning kitchen scraps and yard waste into compost, homeowners can continue to support their plants while protecting the region's waterways from nutrient pollution during the critical summer months.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie resident's home security camera captures burglary in progress, suspect arrested
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A man was arrested Thursday afternoon after a Port St. Lucie resident's home security camera caught him burglarizing an apartment in real time. Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following the incident at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail.

The incident began around 3:38 p.m. when the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. Checking his live camera feed, he spotted a masked man inside his apartment and activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly before returning to tamper with the camera. Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. When Port St. Lucie Police arrived, they found clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary. Thibodeau was transported to the St. Lucie County jail.

hero.headline: Indian River County fertilizer ban begins June 30 to protect waterways
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will need to stop applying fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen to their lawns and landscaping. The restriction takes effect during the rainy season when nutrient runoff poses the greatest threat to local waterways.

The ban is designed to reduce the amount of nutrient-rich runoff that flows into nearby water systems during heavy rainfall. According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, this runoff can trigger algae blooms that damage waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. These blooms create multiple problems for aquatic environments by blocking out the beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In some cases, harmful algae blooms become dense enough to release toxins that threaten human health, animal health and the overall health of ecosystems in the region.

Residents looking for alternatives during the fertilizer restriction period can turn to composting to maintain their landscapes. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, explained that composting is an effective way to add nutrients back into soil and plants. He suggested using a small trash can as a simple and practical composting method that homeowners can easily implement during the ban period.

The three-county fertilizer restriction represents a regional effort to protect water quality during months when rainfall is heaviest and runoff is most likely to carry pollutants into nearby rivers and lagoons. By limiting the use of nitrogen and phosphorus-based fertilizers, local officials hope to prevent the nutrient buildup that fuels destructive algae blooms and maintains healthier conditions for fish, wildlife and human recreation in the area's waterways.
